newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Aid workers see progress with new Afghan rulers.
newsitem.headline: Aid workers see progress with new Afghan rulers.

text.p: A top U.N. aid official said on Thursday he was becoming increasingly optimistic that foreign helpers would find a way to work with Afghanistan's new purist Islamic rulers who intend to impose a strict Moslem way of life.
"The more dialogue we have with them, the less apprehensive we are," Terry Pitzner, the American U.N. aid chief in Kabul, told reporters.

But he said most aid projects in war-torn Afghanistan had halted since the Taleban militia took Kabul a week ago, the high point of their sweep through much of Afghanistan since their movement was born two years ago in refugee camps in Pakistan.

"Most agencies are not functioning and the ones that are are the health agencies," he said after a meeting of aid groups which run medical and food projects and help clear the country of millions of land mines.

He said the groups were putting together a statement to be delivered to Kabul's new rulers, which should be completed on Saturday, to emphasise "our solidarity on human rights issues and the right of women to work".
"The point is that we should address these issues together rather than each group taking its own track," Pitzner said.

The Taleban have decreed that women should stay at home -- though they said women working for the government would be paid until an Islamic way was found for them to return -- and that Islamic sharia law punishments would be imposed on transgressors.

That means amputation for thieves and stoning to death for adulterers. The first Taleban act on entering Kabul was to take communist former president Najibullah out of the U.N. compound where he had been sheltered since he was overthrown in 1992 and execute him.
The bodies of Najibullah and his brother were hanged from a traffic police post near the presidential palace.
Pitzner said the issue of women working was a top priority for the aid agencies, many of which depended on Afghan women.
"We have 40,000 to 50,000 widows in the city who are the sole support of their children. Our projects helping them are dependent on women," he said.
Pitzner said he had met three of Kabul's new ruling six-man shura, or council, and had come away more optimistic that ways would be found around the problems.
"They recognise that our concerns are valid and are willing to address them. We find they are prepared to change policies as soon as they can push them through their machinery," he said.

Pitzner said that meant referring policy changes to Taleban chief Mullah Mohammad Omar in the southern city of Kandahar, and waiting for a response to be sent to the Kabul shura, which would then refer it to a special commission, whose composition and functions were not yet clear.
How much time this would take was equally unclear, Pitzner said, but added: "I am much less apprehensive."
Pitzner said he had been assured by members of the Kabul shura that "women will be in the market place, in the workplace and will be equally educated in Islamic conditions".
This appeared to mean "a separate work space, finding ways of allowing them a role in decision-making in an Islamic way and probably separate transport", he added.
"We will try to hold them to their word," he said.
Pitzner also said he had been assured that the presence of black-turbaned Taleban warriors on the streets of Kabul, where they inspire considerable fear, would be relatively short-lived.
"They say there will be a change when the army has been sent to its barracks or posts outside the city," he said.
Not all women aid workers were sanguine, however.

"I really, really am not looking forward to the next few months," said a European woman staff member with a U.N. agency who said the Taleban officials she had met had all pretended she was not present.
